drills.title: What does this switch print?
drills.promptMd: Trace the execution carefully — pay attention to which `break` statements are present and which are absent.
drills.explanationMd: When `n == 2`, execution jumps to `case 2` and prints `two`. There is no `break` after that case, so execution **falls through** directly into `case 3` and prints `three` as well. The `break` in `case 3` then exits the switch. Fallthrough is the default behavior in C++; only a `break`, `return`, or `[[fallthrough]]` attribute changes it.

drills.title: What does this loop print?
drills.promptMd: Focus on what happens to the loop counter when `continue` fires inside a `for` loop.
drills.explanationMd: In a `for` loop, `continue` skips the rest of the loop body and jumps to the **end-expression** (`++i`), then re-tests the condition. So when `i == 3` the `continue` fires, `++i` still increments `i` to `4`, and the loop proceeds normally. The output is `1 2 4 5`. The "infinite loop" distractor is plausible if you confuse `for` with `while`: in a `while` loop, `continue` would jump straight back to the condition, so if the increment lived in the body after the `continue`, it would be skipped and you could loop forever — but `for`'s end-expression is always safe.

drills.title: Fix the digit-sum loop
drills.promptMd: The function should return the sum of all decimal digits of `n`, but it gives wrong answers for some inputs. Find and fix the off-by-one in the loop condition.
drills.explanationMd: The condition `n > 1` stops the loop when `n` has been reduced to exactly `1`, discarding that last digit. For `n == 7` the loop body runs once (adding 7) and then `n` becomes 0, so it happens to pass — but for `n == 10`, after peeling the `0` digit `n` becomes `1`, the loop exits without ever adding `1`, and the sum is wrong. The fix is `n > 0`: the loop runs until there are no digits left, correctly accumulating the leading digit on every input.

drills.title: Fix the wrong loop kind
drills.promptMd: The function should return `"liftoff"` when called with `0`, but it doesn't. The bug is in the choice of loop — pick the one whose condition is tested *before* the body runs.
drills.explanationMd: A `do while` loop **always executes its body at least once** before checking the condition. So for `n == 0` the body runs, appending `"0 "`, and the result becomes `"0 liftoff"` instead of `"liftoff"`. The fix is to use a plain `while` loop, which tests `n > 0` **before** the body runs — so for `n == 0` the body is skipped entirely and only `"liftoff"` is appended. Use `do while` only when the body must run at least once before there is anything to test.

drills.title: Implement hintText with switch
drills.promptMd: Write `hintText` using a `switch` statement. Map `-1` to `"too low"`, `0` to `"correct"`, `1` to `"too high"`, and any other value to `"invalid"` via the `default` case.
drills.explanationMd: A `switch` evaluates the expression once and jumps to the matching `case` label. Each case ends with a `return` (which also exits the function, so no `break` is needed). The `default` label is the catch-all: it runs when no `case` matches, which is exactly the behavior needed for any code outside `{-1, 0, 1}`. Omitting `default` would leave unexpected codes returning an uninitialized or empty string — a silent bug.
